heading: 2 Budding Civil Servant
src: After the July graduation in 1881, the fellowship broke up. The students finished their four-year course and left for their new positions. One of the members of the audience who observed the graduation ceremony described it in his diary. Early in the afternoon, all of the forty-five students participated in an exhibition of military drill before the roughly 300 visitors. Each of the graduating students delivered an address; each then received a diploma. The applause that followed did not subside for five minutes. Then the valedictorian Kanzô rose to end the ceremony. He thanked the faculty, encouraged the younger students, and finally turned to those of his own class. Great as had been the hardships that they had all endured, he said, these difficulties were as nothing compared with what they could expect in the future. They should stand firm in their resolve to live and to die for the development of Hokkaido. His eloquence educed bleary eyes from the members of his audience. Silence followed his return to his seat.

But sincere intent to remain in Hokkaido did not keep Kanzô there. Immediately upon graduation, he started a career in Sapporo as a specialist in fisheries science. He later recalled that fish had enthralled him even as a child, and he had chosen fisheries science as the subject for his graduation address. Now he suddenly found himself charged with the development of the whole industry in Hokkaido.

In direct contrast to this increase in responsibility, his total income probably shrank, for Kanzô had to pay all his living expenses out of an income only slightly larger than his student stipend, which had come in addition to board, room, and clothes. He rented a house with some of the other church members and grimly attended to his own cooking in a determined attempt at economy, but the loyalty of the group to their little church and its independence presented them with new expenses. With the upperclassmen, the young Christians who had remained so carefully divided into two groups as students united. They then started active evangelization in the community. As its membership gradually increased, the congregation came to dream of acquiring a building. By this time, their enthusiasm had attracted the interest of many missionaries. These missionaries admired the earnest faith of the new Christians, but their decision to establish a united church aggravated feelings of denominational rivalry. Members of the young church had been baptized by missionaries of two denominations: the Episcopalians, who maintained a missionary in Sapporo, and the MethodistEpiscopalians, the official name of the denomination that since 1939 has been known in the United States simply as the “Methodist” Church. The Methodist-Episcopalian missionary at that time resided in Hakodate, 100 mountainous miles to the south. Another man had replaced Harris, the missionary who had ridden from Hakodate to baptize the group to which Kanzô belonged. The students approached Harris’s replacement for a loan to build a church building, and he reluctantly agreed to advance them the large sum of $400.

As they started to build, the church members completed a constitution declaring that they had cut all denominational ties. Henceforth they would be loyal to their local church alone. After some thought, the missionary demanded immediate repayment of the loan.

The letter in which he communicated this demand could not have arrived more inopportunely. The church members received it on Sunday, the 1st of January, in the midst of their final preparations for the dedication of the new building the following Sunday. They had expected the letter to contain a statement acceding to the request of some of them that he drop their names from the rolls of the Methodist-Episcopalian Church. They took his demand for repayment as a challenge and determined to comply as quickly as possible. Their success within the year was no mean feat for a congregation of about fifty, the more wealthy of whom received fifteen dollars per month.

The struggle to repay the money has become famous in Japan as a kind of ecclesiastical declaration of independence. Members of young congregations throughout Japan wanted to be free of mission finance, but no others achieved such a decisive victory in such a short time. As the Japanese nation feared foreign political domination, so the Japanese Christians feared domination in the faith. Financial dependence threatened their freedom more than anything else. The converts usually had little money, and they could always rationalize that to use the funds of others hastened the coming of God’s kingdom. Yet every yen accepted increased their obligation to those from whom they had received it. Given the structures of traditional Japanese society on the subject, it was socially impossible for a self-reliant people to accept funds, however freely given, without feeling bound thereby to the donor. To accept such funds could result only in loss of self-respect and irrational antagonism.

When the offer of funds was linked with denominational rivalry, as it was in this case, the argument that to accept them would aid evangelism also lost its relevance. To Japanese, denominations had grown out of Western history. To allow themselves to become involved in arguments arising from this history would only weaken their faith. The Christians in Sapporo were so few, so determined, and so relatively little influenced by Western denominational thinking that they succeeded where others failed, even though, according to one account, Kanzô had to pawn clothes to pay his share.

Several of the points that they made in their “declaration of independence” show how they saw the issue. In the first place, it says, for graduates of the same school to be split into two rival denominations would be “impossible.” Furthermore, to have two competing churches in a small place like Sapporo would be a “silly plan.” It then turns from the local to the universal to indicate distaste for strictly defined articles of faith and complicated orders of worship. And, finally, it proclaims, Japanese [must] propagate the gospel in Japan without borrowing from foreigners.” Here the young church had set forth the main points of future controversy. Denominations did not fit in with Japanese society or tradition. The money that might accompany their introduction increased the danger of foreign control.

Kanzô led the church in its drive for independence. He also helped its members to draft the constitution. At the same time, he began to lose his enthusiasm for his new employment. He had enjoyed it at first as he travelled on inspection trips to the coastal areas north and east of Sapporo. At various points on these trips, he stopped, interviewed fishermen, and observed their methods and catches. His letters describe how he admired the natural scenery through which he passed. “Rolling waves, hissing winds; echoing forests, thundering cataract [sic]; kingly salmon and beautiful shells ... were ... vivid scenes of might and beauty, love and grace to me.” Throughout his life, Uchimura would attribute his love for unspoiled nature to his Hokkaido experience.

But while he enjoyed the contact with nature, he detested the human contacts. The people he encountered on his travels were “corrupt, degraded, and I can say positively … brutal.” When he returned to his office from his travels, he quickly wrote up reports of what he had learned, but the officers in charge did not seem to know how to use what he had done. As a result, his “present official position” became “loathsome, oppressive, unsatisfactory and corruptive. I have almost nothing to do at present ... We the Christian officers in Sapporo-Ken are great stumbling-blocks to” the others. He concludes that he “must go to Tokio [a common Romanization at the time] this autumn to consider about my future ... 30 yen is too much for doingnothing officers.”

So Kanzô resigned his post after serving less than eighteen months. Apparently, his superiors did not try to hold him to his contract. They probably sensed his feelings and realized that neither he nor they would be happy if they held him to his agreement to remain in Hokkaido. When he arrived in Tokyo, he promptly repaid the last of the loan for the church building three days before the end of the year. The little group had met their obligation and maintained their independence. Uchimura later recorded his pride and his thanks to the mission board for permission to use the money “without interest.”

Seen in retrospect, uncomprehended irony attended this joy at liberation. Kanzô had led the little church to a theological and financial position from which it has not retreated four generations later; however, though he had thus warded off the West, his years learning English and later living as a Westerner made relaxed association with fellow Japanese difficult. On the surface, his symptoms of disaffection resembled those of starting professionals anywhere, but at bottom they differed, for most disaffected graduates shortly settle down into at least a degree of happiness. In December 1882, Kanzô did not know what bothered him. He only followed his restless impulses to the metropolis, where his friends had already begun to make names for themselves.

The Tokyo to which Kanzô returned held many surprises for him. Most of the differences resulted from the increased tempo of Western borrowing. In 1877, as he had set sail for Sapporo, the central government had been directing military operations against a rebellion in far western Kyushu. When he returned, peace had been restored, and the nation had turned its energies again to remaking Japan in the image of the West. The first horse cars had started running up and down the Ginza between Shimbashi and Nihonbashi, and in a little over a year lessons in Western dancing and charity bazaars were to be introduced at the Rokumeikan, a Western-style hall designed to facilitate informal interaction between Japanese and Westerners. At its charity bazaars, the good ladies in their best kimonos and Western dresses filled the hall. One such occasion earned ¥8,000 for a local hospital.

Within this general air of change and Western influence, no others moved with the assurance of the Japanese Christians. They numbered only 5,000, but each year during the preceding few years they had seen their total swell by one-third; there was no reason to believe that this ratio of increase would change. Certain signs portended even faster growth. At several places early in 1883, waves of religious enthusiasm swept over the young. Students at Christian schools were particularly affected. Sometimes for days on end, they groaned at their consciousness of sin and sought the divine presence. Kanzô observed these revivals with skepticism, but to others they seemed to forecast great growth. More encouraging to Kanzô was the reception accorded to Christianity by some government officials. Itô Hirobumi, returning from a trip to Europe, was reported as recommending Christianity and particularly the science associated with it that he believed would help Japan. “He is very anxious about the early evangelization of the whole Empire,” reported Kanzô: “Promising! Promising!”

The confidence of the Christian community best expressed itself at the Third General Conference of Christians held in May 1883. All the Japanese leaders whose opinions and work would characterize Japanese Protestantism until after the First World War attended it. To be present, each took time away from his many duties as pastor, teacher, publisher, or editor. These men were in constant demand. Niijima Jô (1843-90) was the greatest among them; he already administered what would grow into an impressive Christian university in Kyoto. In his address, he prophesied that within ten years all Japan would be Christian and that by the time the new legislative assembly opened in 1890 over half the representatives would be Christian. In the audience along with Kanzô sat the two other men who would live in history as most representative of Christianity in their time. They were Uemura Masahisa and Ebina Danjô. Uemura (1858-1925) was the son of a direct retainer of the Tokugawa family. Less than fifteen years earlier, he had been tending pigs to pay tuition at a mission school. Ebina (1856-1937) was in town from a provincial pastorate at Annaka. At Niijima’s expression of confidence, Uemura is said to have looked at Ebina to indicate his disagreement, and Ebina nodded back. Such dissent reflected a difference in degree rather than conviction. Uemura and Ebina shared the general enthusiasm of the others.

Kanzô found a ready place in this group. His speech at the conference was on “the Birds of the Air and the Lilies of the Field.” In this address, he urged secular scientists to go beyond their narrow specialties to discover evidence of God’s handiwork in the nature with which they dealt. The members of the conference published the speech and thus introduced Kanzô to the capital. The formal photograph taken to commemorate the conference shows Kanzô standing to the right of Niijima and behind the guest of honour, a Korean convert, who represented the international nature of the young Christian movement. He sat next to the patriarch of the Japanese Christians, Tsuda Sen (1837-1909).

Tsuda shortly thereafter employed Kanzô to teach at the school that he had established. It was called the Gakunôsha, or Association for the Study of Agriculture, and it aimed to encourage Christian faith as it imparted modern agricultural techniques. While he taught there, Kanzô continued his activity among the Christians outside the school. He solicited funds for a new Christian publishing house and enlisted members for a national association of Bible students. In Tokyo and removed from the society that Kanzô had dominated in Sapporo, the psychological forces that had found there an equilibrium existed in a new relationship to each other. The churches in Tokyo could not provide the warmth that had come to mean so much to Kanzô, and by his resignation from the government in Hokkaido he had cut himself off from the career that had shown such promise. His family suffered with him. Their demands continued to weigh him down and intensified his need for a clear decision. The Gakunôsha provided no more than a stopgap. He needed a position more in line with his abilities. If only he could find out just what these abilities were! Without friends and prospects, Kanzô felt he was losing control over his environment. Letters from the budding botanist Miyabe and the brooding student of English literature Nitobe intensified his fears, for they indicated that he might both lose their affection and fall behind them professionally.

Both Miyabe and Nitobe had already started up on the escalator of success by which the Meiji government rewarded its loyal servants. They knew that soon they would go abroad to study in the West at government expense. The prospect pleased them, for every educated young man dreamt of travel abroad.

Miyabe had been selected, even before graduation from Sapporo, to go to the university in Tokyo with the expectation that this would lead to study abroad, and he had preceded Kanzô to Tokyo. In the spring of 1883, while Kanzô enthusiastically entered into preparations for the general conference, a fiancée had been found for Miyabe and an engagement announced. She was a distant relative, a Christian, and a Christian school graduate who handled English well and mingled easily with the leaders of Christian society. The date of the marriage was postponed until Miyabe would return from study abroad.

Miyabe asked Kanzô to write to the other Christian brothers in Sapporo about it. Kanzô acceded with a mock seriousness that concealed his own dismay. “You have heard something about little rumours which rage ... [when] our friends ... hunt out wife; but a well filled vessel seems to be exceedingly quiet in such a serious matter. When all attention was directed toward the secret movements of others, when everything was peace and scientific in his behavior,” Miyabe had already made his decision. He later reprimanded Kanzô for his frivolous treatment of so serious a matter. He could not imagine how the announcement of his engagement had threatened Kanzô. Shortly thereafter Miyabe returned to Sapporo and additional research before departure for the United States. In the meantime, Nitobe had arrived from Sapporo, and Kanzô found his presence a consolation that Nitobe’s religious doubts marred only slightly.

Kanzô, then, less than two years after they had all graduated, saw his two closest friends and, we must also remember, competitors moving steadily ahead while he seemed to stagnate. Miyabe’s affections might be taken from him for good, and for a while at least both he and Nitobe would exist an ocean removed. Psychosomatic symptoms appeared at this threat to his inner security. His stomach bothered him, and late in 1883 Kanzô reported “severe throbbings of my heart.” Even before his heart acted up, he had sought relief in two rest cures at hot springs resorts, one in Atami in June and the other in Ikaho three months later.

From inns at each of these places, Kanzô dispatched long letters to Miyabe. Both reflect his need for affection and his inability to decide about his future. From Atami, he wrote, “Dear Love: my father and mother, even, are not so well acquainted with me as thyself.” He continued with phrasing borrowed, perhaps unconsciously, from the twenty-third Psalm: “I need no wife, so long as thou art with me. Thy prayers, thy advice, thy consolation worth more than all I can get in this world.” After a mention of Nitobe, he continued, “let us make ourselves a Christian triplet.”

The 2,000 words in Kanzô’s letter from Ikaho make it one of his longest. It begins in the vein of the Atami letter. In reference to the past, he says, “joy which I enjoyed when I received thy letters, no one but myself knows ... My imagination, heart, intellect, whole self were absorbed in thee. When I wrote letter to thee late in night with joy and tears, and prayers and supplication, my bystanders doubted whether I was insane.” After more of this, he continues to show how rich the friendship of Nitobe and Miyabe makes him. “Poor in treasure, poor in intellect; poor in health, poor in faith; but rich in friends though little in number. I AM FULL, I WANT NO MORE.”

After he has finished this protestation of affection, Kanzô turns almost immediately to the other question that plagued him: his profession. He contemplates, he says, biology, fisheries science, and the Christian ministry. More important than the specific field is his main criterion: “How can I be most serviceable for the sake of God and mankind?” Biology he counts out because Miyabe has told him that he does not have the proper temperament. Fisheries science seems to be the most likely but would put too many burdens on his health, and the ministry is impossible because of his “too great nervousness, rough character, deficient eloquence, as well as weak sensibility.” Having listed the alternatives and found himself wanting in each, he sinks into despair: “When I consider of my future, I always go into tears.” His only recourse is to wait on God. He will do what he is commanded to do, he concludes, while trying to follow Longfellow’s advice to “learn to labor, and to wait.”

These two letters show how completely the tables seemed to Kanzô to have been turned since graduation. He no longer led the group but followed it, dependent upon it for affection, decision, and, it seems, his very being. He says he wants to be part of a “triplet,” but at the same time he recognizes that the other two members stand very well by themselves. He alone needs the support that the continuing presence of the other two would provide.

Kanzô was severely depressed at the two hot springs resorts. Although he craved warmth and affection, he found himself better able to express intimacies in writing rather than in speech. Nitobe was in another inn at Ikaho when Kanzô wrote to Miyabe. Undoubtedly, Kanzô discussed his troubles with Nitobe, but it is doubtful whether Nitobe heard about them in such detail. Like so many others who feel a need for immediate solution to deep psychological problems, Kanzô tried to force himself to remain quiet in the hope that something, someone, would materialize to help him. He decided to learn to wait.

Yet in the last sentences of this marathon letter, he mentions, almost casually, a new topic that reflects recent events. After his reference to Miyabe’s fiancée, he concludes, “remember me brotherly to your Dear One. Let her visit me if she wish. I have now 3 female friends. I can talk with her very freely.”

This introduction of “female friends” into the letter refers to Kanzô’s visit with Nitobe to the provincial city of Annaka, halfway up the pass between Takasaki and Karuizawa to the west of Tokyo. Since Kanzô had spent part of his childhood in Takasaki, the area had connotations of home to him; to a Christian, Annaka had a different but particular significance. As the seat of a daimyo, it had possessed a castle and the attendant advantages, such as superior educational facilities, that this implied. Niijima Jô had left his home there before the end of Tokugawa to travel abroad. Niijima had also sent his most promising pupil, Ebina Danjô, to Annaka as a student evangelist, and Ebina had returned to become the pastor of its church after graduating from Dôshisha, Niijima’s school in Kyoto. Perhaps Kanzô had heard about the church from him at the conference in May. In any case, Kanzô would have wanted to visit Annaka. The church there throve and provided a strong example for others. Many people came forward for baptism; every Sunday 150 to 200 people crowded into their new Western-style church; and they were working on a new and elaborate church government.

Kanzô found in this church shades of the life that he had known in Sapporo. “They are warm, affectionate, brotherly; and above all active. Pleasant was it for me to enjoy a society among warm, lovely Christian community after long exposure to the coldness and indifference of the Metropolitan so-called ‘brothers.’” Among the group was a young lady named Asada Take, with whom Kanzô was soon to find himself impetuously in love.

Thus, the letter in which Kanzô protests his deep affection for Miyabe ends with a note that he too may soon have a fiancée. He shortly did have one, but unlike Miyabe he would not be able to finish his professional training before consummating his courtship.

After his few days in the Ikaho inn, Kanzô returned to Tokyo. One bit of intelligence that greeted his return must have seemed like at least a partial answer to his question of calling. Tsuda had closed the Gakunôsha, and Kanzô needed other employment. He returned to the government, where he was assigned to the Fisheries Section of the Ministry of Agriculture and Commerce. His output during the next ten months reflects real ability and at least fair satisfaction with his work. One of his jobs was to prepare “the catalogue of Japanese fishes, to be inserted in Dr. Chamberlain’s New Dictionary of Japanese and English.” The six monographs that appeared in 1884 reflect a simultaneous interest in several important fields of research. As part of his work, Kanzô prepared studies on salmon, herring, and cod. He also left unpublished another catalogue that, if it had been made available to other researchers, would have materially advanced fisheries science in Japan. He later thought so little of it that he appears to have given it to one of his followers as a memento. These works taken with the research on abalone he did in Sapporo constitute a significant segment of the pioneer work in Japanese fisheries science.

Kanzô could easily have attained status as a scientist equal to that of Miyabe, yet, as his letter from Ikaho indicates, he thought that he could not qualify for such a career. Something drove him into further restless quest, and the careful indecision about a future career shortly gave way to a rash decision about marriage. Kanzô married Asada Take. The marriage lasted only seven months, and the shame of divorce drove him to the United States.

Almost all the information about Take derives from the enthusiastic notices of Kanzô’s first love and the despair of his later disillusion. The picture that they provide seems in the main to be true in spite of its biases. Take was a Christian and had been baptized by Niijima. She had also studied in Dôshisha before transferring to a school in Yokohama. Accomplished in Japanese and knowledgeable enough in English to correspond with Kanzô in it, she appears to have been the type of person both he and his parents would have liked.

But the two of them, particularly his mother, objected strenuously. She distrusted Take’s education and thought that a girl with such training would not become a good daughter-in-law. Possessive, she may not have wanted to receive into her home any girl her son loved. Miyabe and Nitobe also thought that Kanzô should not marry, but even his extreme dependence on them did not restrain him. After almost five months of soul-searching and discussions with them and his family, his parents consented, and he went ahead with the marriage.

Even then he had many doubts, as reflected in a long letter to Miyabe on 18 February 1884: (1) that her “extreme innocence or her recklessness” bothers him, though “to Love’s eyes which are blind, it seems to be” innocence; (2) that the sight of “her cheeks drowned in tears” when he told her of his decision not to marry her has made him change his mind once more; (3) that he considers her a “sister” and that through her marriage to him she becomes Miyabe’s sister too; (4) that he “intended to live apart from her for about a year or more at least” but that her parents’ inability to support her and his mother’s need for assistance in the home have made him decide to marry at once; and (5) that his choice in this matter is important in terms of his own professional future: “A wife well used is a decided help in our future career; misused, a grand obstacle.” His diary entry for 14 March – over three weeks later – indicates that he read the life of the selfless British prison reformer John Howard “with tears.” This does not sound like the reaction of a twenty-three-year-old who faced marriage in two weeks, but by then he may have felt trapped, for the time to change his mind had passed. On 28 March, they were united by Kanzô’s missionary friend, M.C. Harris.

A twenty-four-year-old American woman who attended the wedding left us her impressions. The bride was “a pleasant-faced roly-poly young woman of twenty” and the bridegroom “one of the most intellectual, interesting Japanese young men I have ever met.” When Harris pronounced them husband and wife, “some present fancied they heard a giggle from the bride,” but because she was a Christian “no doubt their’s [sic] will be a happy Christian home.”

Kanzô seems to have been happy as a bridegroom even though three days later he confided in Miyabe that he had “to exercise not a little energy to check her [Take’s] ‘constitutional enthusiasm.’” Two months later research took him to Sapporo alone; there he described Take to his friends in glowing terms. When he returned, he discovered that all was not right between Take and her mother-in-law, and, when Kanzô took his mother’s side, Take did not meekly accept his rebukes. A few months later he became convinced “by the testimonies of 4 or 5” that “she whom I trusted to be my helper, my consolator, my coworker, was found to be a rascal, a wolf in sheep’s skin.” Although she was pregnant, Kanzô asked her brother to take her home, yet when she left with him, one source says, Kanzô fell down on his face and cried.

After Take left the Uchimura home and gave up thoughts of reconciliation with Kanzô, she married again and settled down near her family home. She gave the daughter that was born a few months later to her brother. As she developed, the daughter became one of Uchimura’s spiritual disciples. His letters reflect an interest in her development both pastoral and fatherly.

Kanzô must have puzzled Take. His self-conscious religiosity and concern for calling must have seemed pompous. Her own need for affection may have prompted her to attempt to arouse him. Kanzô probably could not respond with the warmth that she desired. Studies with Thematic Apperception Tests in Japan seem to indicate that in many cases, when a young man brings a wife into a Japanese home, his feelings toward his mother prevent him from a free sexual relationship with his wife. He expects his wife to mother him and sees any free attitudes toward sex as an expression of untoward licentiousness. Whether or not factors of this sort influenced Kanzô, it is certain that the six weeks or so when his wife remained in Tokyo alone with his mother must have intensified their mutual antipathy and made it more difficult for him to choose between them.

There is also little doubt that Kanzô thought his marriage had hurt his career prospects. His tears over the Howard biography may have welled up from the realization that his choice to marry precluded the possibility of glorious sacrifice for others similar to that of Howard. When he wrote to Miyabe that he “intended to live apart from” Take, it appears that what he wanted was what Miyabe had: a fiancée of whom his parents approved and to whom he could look forward as he finished his training.

Finally, it appears to have taken little to convince Kanzô of her guilt. The “testimonies of 4 or 5” – and nothing more is known of who they were or what they said – confirmed unspecified worries that he had felt since the marriage but had blamed, he said, on himself. Although he implies that she had been unfaithful to him, there is no evidence to substantiate such an assumption other than a vague reference to a letter or letters that she may have written. When he first met Take, her enthusiasm and warmth had attracted him. In marriage, the same characteristics seem to have threatened him and confirmed his mother’s earlier misgivings. It is not impossible that, for a variety of reasons, he himself did not understand that he magnified some chance comments by Take out of proportion. All that is certain is that the scars of the divorce never healed sufficiently so that he could mention it in a career otherwise marked by frequent references to the events of his life.

After Take left in the fall of 1884, Kanzô’s prospects seemed bleak. His one great decision had gone bad; in an attempt to avoid further decision, Kanzô accepted the advice of friends “to leave the country for a moment, and to find relief in America.” The divorce had further limited his professional opportunities for the future. Many members of the Christian community could not understand his intractable attitude toward Take. His decision to flee rather than to reconcile with her cost him their sympathy. Normally, he would have left for America with the blessing of his colleagues, but now he went to escape their censure and so became particularly sensitive to the experiences that lay ahead of him.

Finally, Kanzô had violated a cardinal ethical principle of his childhood through his insistence on marriage: he had not followed his parents’ advice. He recognized that they had consented only because of his persistence, and he came to believe that he had contravened both the traditional Japanese attitudes toward parents and the Christian’s duty, as he saw it, to the will of God.

Kanzô acted quickly. Within little over a week after he informed Miyabe of the divorce, he had received letters of introduction from American friends, exhausted his savings and apparently mortgaged his future to buy a ticket, packed the collection of Japanese poems (waka) that Miyabe had given Take and him for a wedding present, and boarded a ship for the United States. In later years, Uchimura believed that at this time God had led him “into the wilderness” on a spiritual quest that was to last ten to fifteen years. Yet, by a curious alchemy of ambition and error, Kanzô had come out ahead once more in his competition with Miyabe. He had experienced the fruits, however bitter, of marriage ahead of Miyabe, and now he left for the United States before Miyabe. Nitobe had gone ahead a few months earlier. Although Kanzô left for America in headlong flight, what now seemed to him a place of refuge would have seemed to most of his contemporaries the exciting land where each could fulfill his or her dreams. The others on the ship had high hopes. Those who bid them good-bye could not but wish that they were going too.

Well might they have envied Kanzô. He had a more impressive trip than most. It started with a rail journey across the United States via Ogden, Utah, to the town of Elwyn in suburban Philadelphia. There he found employment in a boarding school for mentally retarded children. He also received frequent invitations to dine and to speak. The people he met possessed generous means and interested themselves in other lands and their people’s problems. Isaac Kerlin, the director of the hospital where Kanzô worked, took a personal interest in him. He even shepherded Kanzô to Washington in the summer of 1885. There the two of them attended the annual meeting of the Conference of Charities and Correction. Kerlin was one of the moving spirits behind the conference, and through his introductions Kanzô mingled with the leaders of the profession for a week. The experience would have pleased most graduate students. Kanzô briefly addressed a meeting and later went with Kerlin to the White House, where President Cleveland “grasped my hand and congratulated me on coming to America.” During the following days, Kanzô visited the director of the Smithsonian Institution and government fisheries experts. Kerlin had gone to real pains for his young friend.

Kanzô left Elwyn after his return from Washington. Once again his spiritual concerns had induced physical symptoms. He first rested for two weeks in Gloucester, Massachusetts. On the way, he had a few hours in New York City that enabled him to see the Brooklyn Bridge and other sights. He arrived at Gloucester at the height of the blueberry season; there he let the summer breezes refresh him and ate the berries until his “lips became black.”

After his two weeks at the summer resort, Kanzô went to Boston and thence Amherst. He spent the rest of his time in the States either there or at nearby Hartford, except for occasional trips to Boston and Elwyn. He extended one of the latter trips to Maryland and was received by the governor.

For most of Kanzô’s contemporaries, it would have seemed an exciting interlude and formed the basis for many recollections after they returned home. Yet Uchimura did not capitalize on the exhilarating aspects of his experience when he returned to Japan; his stay in the United States remained in his memory and remains in the historical image of him as a period of spiritual turmoil.

Out of the places that Kanzô visited, three assumed importance in retrospect, and of the people he met four made decisive contributions to his development. The places were Elwyn, Gloucester, and Amherst; the people are introduced in connection with his sojourns in these towns.

Kanzô went to Elwyn with an introduction from an American friend in Tokyo, the brother of the young lady who had described Kanzô’s wedding in her diary. He wrote to an acquaintance in Philadelphia on Kanzô’s behalf, and this man in turn introduced his young visitor to Kerlin. Kanzô was very dejected when he arrived. His letters home announcing his arrival show how greatly he had lost stature in his own eyes. When he addressed his father, he used for the first-person pronoun “ji,” a humilific that clearly indicates one’s dependence. It might be translated as “your helpless infant.” Suddenly once again a child, he had changed from official and busy churchman to penitent and frightened sinner. And once again he had become an eager neophyte at the feet of the Americans, whom he considered bearers of a superior culture.

Ten years later Uchimura wrote that he had entered “hospital service with somewhat the same aim as that which drove Martin Luther into his Erfurth convent.” This statement is true in terms of motivation: Kanzô in Elwyn feared the wrath of God and sought to avoid it by the subjugation of his flesh. A casual observer would not have suspected the inner turmoil that he felt, for his work load made few demands on him. It included “to be a nightwatch every other night, and to such [sic; teach?] the lowest grade of Imbeciles 3 hours a day in walking, climbing ladders, and using dumbbells.” As a self-imposed penance, he undertook some of the more degrading jobs, such as feeding and cleaning up after the children, but his duties left him with much time to read and ruminate on the weaknesses of human flesh, so many unfortunate examples of which surrounded him.

Kanzô read voraciously. When one of the matrons warned him with kindly intent that he read “too much,” he reacted with a sense of disbelief that it was possible to read too much. He then used the remark to illustrate the low cultural level of some Americans. Books became his only friends, he said, yet in the same letters he indicated that he had numerous invitations to dinner. The Americans he met seem to have tried to make him welcome, and they would have been surprised to hear him later compare his experience to life in a monastery. Kerlin in Elwyn would probably have liked Kanzô to consider him a friend. Kanzô came to admire him, but he considered the relationship not that of friendship but that of pupil to master or son to father. Kerlin became one of Kanzô’s American parents. He was a physician who concerned himself with social welfare and treatment for the mentally retarded. In 1862, President Lincoln had asked him to establish a colony near Washington for the escaping slaves, who had crowded in on it. Smallpox had broken out, and the plan had been abandoned, but Kerlin had remained in Washington in charge of the Sanitary Commission for the District of Columbia. He had moved to the Elwyn hospital shortly after the end of the war.

Kerlin knew mental disorders and seems to have sensed quickly the general nature of the problem that plagued Kanzô. He believed, Uchimura later recalled, that mental health depended in part on physical health and made it his business to look after Kanzô’s bodily needs while affording the young man time to wrestle with his spiritual problems. To Kanzô, Kerlin seemed the embodiment of humanity and trust. The young Japanese later remarked with half disbelief that he had been given his own key upon arrival. Kerlin also entrusted him one day with a $5,000 bond to deliver to a broker’s office in Philadelphia. The memory of this incident later prompted an essay by Kanzô on the faith that American mentors have in their disciples.

At first in Elwyn, Kanzô felt deeply depressed. He frequently mentioned the failure that had driven him from Japan. Writing to Nitobe in Baltimore, he admits that he has sinned against “God, ... parents, and not less to thee.” Later he adds, “if to err is human, I am intensely so.” Letters from his wife or her family in Annaka he read once and burned.

Gradually, Kerlin’s therapy began to work. Kanzô’s depression lessened, and the concerns that had beset him before his marriage reassumed their former ascendance. Kanzô discovered that mortification of the flesh of the type that he undertook at Elwyn had not worked. As always for him, religious enlightenment, even though communicated in a flash of inspiration, followed prolonged rational exercises rather than physical labour or emotional frenzy.

Kanzô found the material for such exercises in the Old Testament. Reverend Harris, his missionary friend, had suggested Hosea apparently shortly after the divorce. In Hosea, the infidelity of Israel is compared to adultery. In the end, the harlot Israel is reconciled to her husband God as the errant wife is reconciled to Hosea. Kanzô could not accept the formula of reconciliation in his own case, but Harris’s suggestion of an Old Testament passage seems to have led him to read all of the Old Testament for the first time. The prophets particularly appealed to him. They shed new light on the problem of the individual and responsibility both to God and to his or her nation. The sense of personal responsibility developed into responsibility for his nation. Kanzô began to wonder if prophets might not be born in the modern world, in his own Japan. The seeds of this development lay in Elwyn, but the fruit did not appear until ten years later.

Government leaders in Meiji Japan seem in general to have concerned themselves with national goals at the expense of their own careers. Perhaps they did so more than most other leaders in most nations and periods of history. The national position of Japan and the loyalties of these men within Japan conjointly fostered this attitude. Kanzô, who considered himself one of them, felt concern for Japan as a duty. His experience in the United States intensified this concern. Uchimura did not address the subject directly in any of his writings. If his experience in the United States is to be understood, it is necessary to use the few sources that remain from his time there in the light of his earlier development.

Kanzô’s letters to friends at this time and Uchimura’s later writings addressed to foreigners return frequently to the theme of acceptance. Most conspicuous are his references to the hurt that Kanzô received when he was considered a “Chinaman.” One is tempted to smile at this as an example of racial discrimination in the objection to it. It is certain that the modern Japanese has not shared forebears’ positive identification with China, but this feeling of superiority toward Chinese is, for the most part, a later development. Although perhaps some Japanese felt superior in 1885, objective events did not confirm their assumptions for ten years. Kanzô’s references had another significance.

The Chinese with whom Kanzô and his friends were confused were coolies, workers who had been brought in from the southeast coast of China as docile and cheap labour. Typically, Kanzô was mistaken for a laundryman. “A well-clad gentleman sharing the same seat with me in a [street] car asked me to have my comb to brush his grizzly beard; and instead of a thanks which we in heathendom consider appropriate on such an occasion, he returned the comb saying, ‘Well John, where do you keep your laundry shop?’” Kanzô does not seem to have objected to this identification – or even the effrontery of such requests – as such. He did object, however, to what identification as a Chinese implied: that anyone with an Oriental face, no matter how well dressed or demeaned, was a menial. This attitude bespoke to him contempt for all his education and all the efforts of his nation at self-improvement, for if, no matter how they had learned the rules the Western way, they could not be accepted for what they had become, they could ultimately expect no justice. The results of disillusion brought on by such discrimination are familiar in the lives of Gandhi and other Indians. Their later careers indicate the international consequences of slights that objectively would have seemed of little consequence. Kanzô in 1885 first felt the fear and frustration that accompany such a discovery. For much of his later life, he wrestled with its implications.

But consideration beneath the station to which he felt entitled as an individual was not the only evidence of discrimination that Kanzô encountered. He also felt that in some quarters he was treated more as a symbol than as a person. This is how he interpreted the treatment that he received as a convert at the hands of missionary societies. He thought that he and other foreign converts in the United States were herded around to missionary meetings to describe their conversions. He later called those who accepted such treatment “tamed rhinoceroses.” He wrote that the rhinoceros was asked at such meetings to describe his conversion much as a circus animal might be obliged by his keeper to perform. A local newspaper carried an article while Kanzô was studying in Amherst that demonstrated another aspect of the same phenomenon. The article described coming activities at the church that Kanzô attended. They included this one: “The young women’s missionary society [will] hold a supper and sale of fancy articles, home-made candy, etc. A Japanese wedding will be one of the attractions.” To Kanzô, with his particular sensitivity to weddings, the display of a Japanese wedding like a sideshow would have brought intense pain.

To use the word discrimination here may seem to place unfair demands on its definition. Actions of this sort that make foreign visitors feel uneasy do not arise from contempt. On the contrary, they arise from a well-intentioned desire to share of one’s bounty, to learn, and to express affection. These were without doubt the major motives behind the nineteenth-century missionary movement to all parts of the world. But to treat a guest this way reflects deep misunderstanding that can be interpreted by a sensitive heart as lack of acceptance. The young tamed rhinoceros and the participants in the “Japanese wedding” may believe that they are expected by their hosts to act in a way not required of those whom the hosts really care about. These requests can thus seem to reflect an attitude of superiority almost as complete as that felt by those who would make of all Orientals Chinese coolies.

Even among the wealthy philanthropists of Philadelphia, Kanzô seems to have sensed an implicit rejection. By their very wealth, these people impressed upon him his own precarious financial situation. They acted as a mirror for the poverty that he remembered at home. The wealthy in any land have the means to interest themselves in foreign guests, and the philanthropists among them can aid any cause immensely. Yet by their opulence and generosity, they often put off those whom they wish to aid. Kanzô reports how the good Christians of Philadelphia made him feel his own lack of money. When Kerlin suggested that they visit President Cleveland, Kanzô’s first reaction was that his clothes, made in Japan, could not measure up to the occasion. Wistar Morris, the man whom Kanzô had first visited in Philadelphia and who had introduced him to Kerlin, possessed great wealth. When Kanzô wondered in the spring of 1885 which of various alternatives he should select upon leaving Elwyn, the Morrises offered to pay for his expenses to medical school. He wrote that they “bind me ... by their too much kindness” and that he did not want to accept their money. His concern, though unspoken, for what they might have required in return made him reject their help.

Kanzô’s experiences contributed to the melancholy caused by his indecision and probably increased his tendency to identify with the prophets who aimed to save their nation. His experience in America taught Kanzô that he would never be anything but a Japanese. It also increased his doubts that Japanese could ever, in the final analysis, truly equal Americans.

By the spring of 1885, after five months in Elwyn, Kanzô had recovered from his original depression enough to consider his professional future once more. He decided on more study, but he found that concern over the choice of a school and a specialty induced more spiritual turmoil. At this point, the energetic Niijima Jô, who had founded the Dôshisha in Kyoto, where both Ebina and Uchimura’s former wife had studied, stepped in to help Kanzô. Niijima, on a trip to the United States, went to Baltimore to visit Nitobe, who told him about Kanzô’s melancholy, and Niijima “sent a telegram to him at once.” It suggested that they meet. Niijima’s visit must have seemed providential to Kanzô. He met the older man in Philadelphia, and they started a correspondence that lasted over the summer. It shows how only another of his own countrymen could help Kanzô when the various Americans from whom he had sought advice had failed.

Niijima was about eighteen years older than Kanzô. In America as a student, Niijima had attended the preparatory school Phillips Academy in Andover and then moved on to Amherst College. There he had come to know its president, Julius Seelye, and had developed the ambition to establish a Japanese Amherst in Kyoto. He had fulfilled this ambition at the cost of his health. He journeyed to the United States at this time to recuperate. In spite of his own fatigue, Niijima responded with understanding and patience when he heard of Kanzô’s troubles. He knew the problems that conversion and residence in the United States brought to a Japanese, and he probably knew the details of the divorce. No one else could have helped Kanzô more. In addition to his spiritual assistance, Niijima performed the practical services of introducing Kanzô to Amherst and obtaining for him a scholarship there.

Kanzô’s letters to Niijima indicate the totality of his dependence, and their poor English reflects the turmoil within his mind. He wrote the first one about a month after the two met. In the interval, Kanzô had travelled to Washington and while there had written a letter to his former wife’s brother that contains the best statement on the divorce. After reviewing the facts from Kanzô’s point of view, it demands that the matter be considered settled. To compose it must have occasioned much pain. When Kanzô addressed Niijima five days later, he concluded, “my head is exceedingly confusing: hence the bad English and general confusion. Letters from Home extremely discouraging. A Wicked woman trying to torment my parents.” For two months, he vacillated between various possibilities. The rhetoric of his letters recalls Saint Augustine or Saint Paul.

> With regard to my future, I have thought over and over again, and still ... I cannot come to any definite conclusion. If I take my own way I am afraid I might make a mistake again. On one hand, I almost shrink from entering such an honorable duty as Ministry with all the insufficiencies and wants of characters [sic] and faith. On the other hand, my heart has been so trained that nothing short of the Eternal Love of God can satisfy it. Poor me, if I cannot preach the Gospel; but wretched man I am, I cannot be what I wish to be. So with the mind, I follow the law of spirit; and with the flesh, the law of sin. Who can deliver me from this flesh of sin?

Niijima responded with direct advice. He feared that Kanzô’s ascetic meditation would affect his body. “It is good sensation but if anyone goes too far in that way the result may be seriously destructive. Can’t you lay aside the books of Job & Jeremiah for a while & try to read the book of Daniel & also Paul’s missionary work in The Acts?” Kerlin agreed that Kanzô’s spiritual difficulties threatened his health and recommended the trip to Gloucester.

In Elwyn, Kanzô had worked through acts of penance and incessant reading to overcome the shame of the divorce. Now the other great problem – his calling, specifically what course he should take in the immediate future – appears to have driven him from Elwyn to a spot where no one knew him. In Gloucester, he could meditate alone while he refreshed himself after the self-imposed rigours of Elwyn. His tired body enjoyed the blueberries, and his mind at last found the peace to decide on his future. While he considered this question of career, he actually started on what would become his career: writing about ethical questions out of the depths of his experience. He penned an article in English. Mrs. Harris helped him to publish it, and the royalties paid for the two-week sojourn on the coast.

The article was called “Moral Traits of the ‘Yamato Damashii.’” That Kanzô could muster reserves even at such a time to produce a work worthy of publication in English reflects his basic strength and resilience. Alone where no one knew him, he found the creative resource to support himself for a few weeks with the tool that he had so laboriously mastered.

His letters to Niijima and his father reflect the terms in which Kanzô considered his professional decision. To Niijima, he is a spirit in torment over the responsibility of unavoidable choice. To his father, Yoshiyuki, he carries on his shoulders the weight of the nation, as in a passage where he demonstrates at once how his sojourn in Gloucester provided him with a kind of self-analysis and how the various strands of his past converged on him at that moment. The letter first tells about his trip. It mentions former President Grant’s funeral and then suddenly turns to international relations. Russia and England had been squabbling over the Afghan border, and rumour had it that trouble would break out between Russia and China. In either case, it appeared that the lands of Central Asia would shortly become the stage for world conflict.

> My body actually shakes when I consider that in the not-distant future our country may meet a similar fate. At the time of the Restoration your heart ached with concern over the fate of Takasaki han; can Kanzô face up to these tremendous changes? Kanzô has no strength, no knowledge; therefore he wants to burnish his spirit and serve his country with a spear of righteousness that neither a Krupp gun can demolish nor other blade approach. If it comes to a decision based upon warships or gun smoke, our country will disappear like a flickering flame before a puff of wind.

This passage indicates that the seven-year-old Kanzô had received, at the time of the Restoration, both a clear impression of national peril and a sense of his father’s inability as he faced that peril. Kanzô even remembered that his father had turned to him for support. There is little wonder that Kanzô had suffered under such a sense of responsibility and had sought mechanisms to lighten it.

The recollection of the specific event at this time is also significant. Kanzô had reacted to the divorce with the sense that he had sinned against his parents and his heritage. The article that he sent off to Mrs. Harris at about the same time he wrote to his father said, in part, “to the Japanese no relation can be greater than the sacred relation of child to parent. Infidelity in this regard is, in Japan, synonymous with immorality.” He now accepted his family and all that it meant once more, yet neither his father nor his nation seemed strong enough to cope with the urgent and continuing crises that they faced. The attitude of the Americans he had met had indicated that he as a Japanese, even though a Christian, was not one of them but an Asian, like any Chinese or Afghan. His fellow Japanese must be on guard lest they suffer at the hands of Westerners as the Chinese and Afghans had suffered. Kanzô would take up the vigil for his country and assume the responsibility for this tremendous task. As he had read the Old Testament in Elwyn, he had learned that the heroes on Earth were the prophets who had taken upon themselves just such tasks on behalf of their nation. God had assisted them as long as they had remained faithful to him. They had served their countries as Kanzô would his, “with a spear of righteousness.”

Here at last Kanzô’s triangle of emotions fell into new equilibrium. Emotional satisfaction he would find at home among his own people according to traditional ways. The responsibility that had so burdened him had become more specific. He must save his nation and his generation, an aweinspiring calling that also gave him free rein for his ambitions. And to control the fears that this prospect conjured up, he would find a new spear: the religion of the Old and New Testaments. Kanzô would need help to prepare himself for his task, and he took Niijima’s advice to seek it in Amherst. He left Gloucester, he wrote to Niijima, “with a new spirit. The greatest burden of my soul was cast into the bay of Gloucester never to be even looked at” again.

During these two weeks, as Kanzô ate blueberries, his search for identity ended. There is no further information on exactly what happened. There may have been a dramatic revelation or sense of calling that suddenly clarified everything. More tribulations faced him. Many of them recalled symptoms similar to those he had faced frequently before, but they did not include the problem either of basic vocational dedication or of national identity. To borrow the younger Otis Cary’s phrase, the Gloucester experience formed the core of Kanzô’s “summer of decision.” Kanzô had made up his mind once and for all, and his later life can be understood only in the light of this decision.

Kanzô went quickly on to Amherst. There he found that Julius H. Seelye, the president of Amherst, expected him. Kanzô would come to consider Seelye his spiritual father. Contemporaries regarded Seelye as a giant, and the president at Amherst eighty years later still regarded him as one of his most illustrious predecessors.

Seelye had “colossal proportions, a large frame and tawny beard that made him conspicuous at any gathering.” Kanzô also noted these proportions with awe. More important to him, however, were the eyes and the warmth in Seelye’s initial greeting. “He made me feel I should treat him more as a friend than stand in awe of him as my teacher.” Seelye, for his part, gained a real respect for the young Kanzô over the next two years. He was later quoted as having said, “I consider that Mr. Uchimura had the finest mind with which I ever came in contact.”

This was high praise from a man who daily met so many first-rate scholars and himself possessed such a good mind. Although Seelye was not an original thinker, he had an amazing memory for details. In 1872, on his way to India, he had read a history of Japan and stopped over there. Fourteen years later he answered a chance question on the history of Japan with a wealth of detail. Kanzô listened with astonishment.

For all his own intelligence, Seelye interested himself primarily in developing capable citizens out of the young men who came to Amherst. He showered particular care and affection on those with interest in religious problems. No matter how grave the doubts, he received those who suffered because of them with warmth and affection. Seelye, generally aloof, five years a widower, and aging, no doubt enjoyed the contact with these earnest youthful minds. None of the students appears to have been a more frequent visitor to Seelye than Kanzô.

From one such meeting, Kanzô returned with the inspiration that gave him new confidence in his resolve. He believed in the reality of the doctrine of atonement: that Jesus had already taken upon himself the sins of humanity and in particular the sins of Kanzô. Here he found the assurance that he need no longer fear the results of decision. He had now made up his mind what he wanted to do and had the confidence with which to begin it. Seelye had led Kanzô to this understanding. Many years later Uchimura reminisced, “Seelye called me in one day and said, ‘Uchimura, you shouldn’t always look within yourself. Why do you not cease this introspection and look up at Jesus who atoned for your sins on the cross? You are like a small boy who plants a tree and then every day pulls it up by the roots to observe its development.’” Seelye had intuitively set his finger on the source of the problem. He had also provided the spark that transformed into conviction the formless aspirations that Kanzô had brought with him.

Amherst College and its surroundings were strongly Puritan. The president and others in it embodied both the strengths and the weaknesses of that point of view. On an average morning, Seelye might lead the freshman class in calisthenics, then that evening attend a meeting at the First Church to hear a committee report that one of the church’s members had been “playing billiards” and that he “had joined the church for pecuniary motives.” Church affairs also called Seelye out of Amherst. He was one of three clergymen invited to judge the famous Andover heresy trial that took place during Kanzô’s last year at Amherst. In cases like those of alleged heresy and communal concern for personal motivation, Seelye acted as a moderating influence within the community. He alone on the board of three voted for the acquittal of the Andover professor of ecclesiastical history whose published views some people considered too liberal. Although most of Seelye’s Amherst colleagues would probably have agreed with him on this point, they all worked within the confines of a tight society whose strictures they generally accepted.

For those who shared their assumptions, Amherst provided excellent surroundings for study and learning. Kanzô encountered fine teachers and greatly broadened his intellectual horizons. Among the subjects that he studied, languages and history excited him the most. In two years, he learned enough German to enjoy Goethe’s Faust and enough Greek and Hebrew to spend a summer reading the Gospel of John and selections from a compilation of Jewish writings. Forty years later he wrote Greek-script marginalia on some of his English-language reference works. In history at Amherst, Kanzô recalls, he did not have to start from scratch, for he had long enjoyed it. He later noted that he had read two of the general texts for world history eight and ten times respectively before he entered Amherst. There he learned both more facts and a specific attitude toward history: that it expressed God’s will and should be studied to learn that will. Kanzô became particularly interested in biography as the means to benefit from the experiences of great people.

In Amherst, Kanzô also failed a course for the first time in his life. It was philosophy. Here, like many Japanese, he found the theories of knowledge and logic wholly beyond him. In general, he enjoyed abstract studies the least. For him, knowledge had to be practical and immediately applicable to his concerns. The sciences and history demonstrated God’s handiwork in the world, languages enabled humans to read how God had spoken to them, but John Locke’s philosophy of learning seemed nothing more than a waste of time.

Uchimura later said little else about the general intellectual environment at Amherst, but he could not have avoided the influences of a pervasive way of life that was dying. The aging Ralph Waldo Emerson had spoken at the college in 1879, shortly after Seelye became president. Seelye served as an honorary pall bearer at the funeral of Emily Dickenson, the frail and lonely poetess of nature, who lived across the street from the college and died the spring after Kanzô arrived.

To judge from the mature Uchimura’s writings, Kanzô spent all his time with books and professors. He hardly refers to other students at all. The few exceptions reflect thinly veiled condescension. In this general lack of interest in his colleagues, the letters that remain show that in Amherst Kanzô found one student friend who corresponded with him the rest of his life. The student was Alfred L. Struthers.

Struthers went on from Amherst to divinity school with Uchimura. Later he became the pastor of a church in Minneapolis. Uchimura’s letters to Struthers reflect deep respect and provide poignant insights into Uchimura’s first years after his return to Japan.

Amherst granted Kanzô a degree in science after two years of residence, and he left it to enroll for further training at Hartford Theological Seminary. There the professionalism of the students and the irrelevance of much course material disturbed him. Casual references to sermons and pastorates in terms of the income that they would provide seemed to belie the high calling of the ministry. The course material, with its emphasis on the techniques of the pastoral profession, also contained little of relevance for one consumed with concern over how to preserve his nation. If Christianity meant only what it seemed to mean to the other students, it could not provide the strength that Kanzô needed from it.

He turned to read the lives of great Christians. Over twenty years later, Uchimura recalled how he read at this time a biography of the missionary David Livingston. “I went through the big volume of more than five hundred pages in three days of continuous reading. I read it and wept. I too wanted to become such a person, and I determined that I should.” Shortly thereafter insomnia took hold of him. He toyed with becoming a missionary to India or China but decided after a talk with the Kerlins to return home. He sailed from New York, passed over the Isthmus of Panama, visited the Harrises in San Francisco, stopped in Vancouver, and reached Tokyo in May 1888.

Kanzô tells about his return in a letter to an American friend, David C. Bell. It was the first in a correspondence that continued almost forty years until shortly before Uchimura’s death. Kanzô had met Bell in a horse car, the predecessor of a streetcar, during his visit to Washington. They briefly met once more in the United States, and Bell much later visited Uchimura for a few days in Japan. Other than that, their friendship depended on regular correspondence. Bell saved the letters that he received from Japan, and they form one of the best sources we have on Uchimura’s life. Whereas the letters to his Japanese friends are intimate and informal, those to Bell read almost like reports on work accomplished and books read. The two groups complement each other.

Bell was the last of the Americans who helped Uchimura and seemed to him to represent the best in the American tradition. Twenty years Uchimura’s senior, Bell was a Minneapolis banker and Sunday school teacher who belonged to the church pastored by Struthers. Bell had a personal interest in problems of faith and evangelization and sent the younger man books and articles about Christianity that he himself had enjoyed. Uchimura expressed frequent thanks for them. In at least one case, he was deeply influenced by something that Bell had sent him, though Bell’s choices did not mould Uchimura’s thinking as much as confirm it. Bell stood more in the position of sympathetic friend and counsellor than spiritual guide.

The Americans who have been introduced so far – Reverend and Mrs. Harris, Kerlin, Seelye, Struthers, and Bell – along with classmates in Japan were the individuals whom Uchimura felt influenced him the most. With the exception of one German and one Englishman whom Uchimura met early in the twentieth century, these were the people his own age or older for whom he felt particular respect and warmth. The only others with whom he would feel a sense of well-being for any length of time were the disciples who began to gather around him at the turn of the century.

Niijima and Bell were both about half a generation older than Uchimura. Niijima’s death within five years after Uchimura returned to Japan precluded the further development of their friendship, but one suspects that they could not have worked together in any case. Niijima was too close to Uchimura. He knew too much of Uchimura’s past. They also disagreed on a number of points that Uchimura considered essential. Although in constant communication with Bell, Uchimura did not refer to him at length in any of his writings. Neither of these men therefore forms a part of the tradition that has grown up around Uchimura’s memory in Japan.

The cases of Mrs. Harris, Doctor Kerlin, and President Seelye are very different. These three appear frequently both in Uchimura’s writings and in those of his followers. Each was about a generation older than Kanzô, and each befriended him with an almost parental consideration at a time of crisis. For a while at least, Kanzô looked upon each of them as a parent. Mrs. Harris, with her constant warmth, encouragement, and understanding, won a place that his own mother never achieved. And Kerlin along with Seelye are referred to with the warmth one usually reserves for a father. Seelye in particular seems to have provided both affection like that of Kanzô’s blood father, Yoshiyuki, and spiritual strength much greater than Yoshiyuki’s.

Yet these persons in reality were always distant. Kanzô met Mrs. Harris only infrequently and then almost always at his suggestion and when he wanted a favour. He lived near the Kerlins for only five months when other concerns preoccupied him. And Seelye was a busy college president and community leader. Furthermore, by 1909 all of these persons had died. In no case did any of them have to discipline Kanzô. They existed in memory almost entirely as benevolent figures who sympathized with his aspirations. He had chosen his surrogate parents carefully to fit his particular needs. They always supported and helped him.

All three adopted relatives belonged to a particular type of American, what Richard Hofstadter refers to as “genteel reformers.” These reformers were the heirs of the vigorous eighteenth-century American Puritanism. Committed to the ethics of a Protestant agrarian society, they rapidly became less representative of ruling currents in their homeland. As individuals, their intellects and accomplishments compelled respect, but as forces in society they steadily lost influence. They often considered themselves faithful to a golden tradition, return to which would solve the world’s problems. It would not be difficult for a strong Biblicist to identify them with the loyal remnant of Israel in the Old Testament.

This Uchimura later did. Those things about the United States that he disliked became for him examples of defection from an ideal. He believed that he had observed life based on this ideal in Elwyn and Amherst. Long after those who had personally exemplified it to him had left the scene, he continued to believe that a few individuals in the United States remained true to the ideal. As long as he remained confident that their spiritual descendants carried on the tradition, he had a locus for that part of his affections and need for security that had no home in Japan. They had helped him to burnish his “steel,” and they would help him before God. When he became convinced that even the loyal remnant had ceased to exist, he faced a spiritual crisis at least as grave as that which he had faced in Gloucester. Only during the First World War would Uchimura face up to that disillusion. On return home in 1888, his concern centred on the attempt to apply his Christian ideals in heathen Japan. Back in Japan, Kanzô felt as if he had awakened from a dream: “For a fortnight I was in a state of trance, as it were, amazed at the singular people among whom I came, and of whom, I know, I was one. I had to struggle hard to reaccommodate myself to the Japanese mode of living, and it was indeed a very trying experience.” Kanzô attempted with little success to persuade his friends that his experience had not changed him as much as they suspected it had. “They imagined that I lost much of my passionate love for my country by living many years in America. But, I thank God that I went out of my country as a Japanese, and returned as a Japanese.”

Since Kanzô had left in 1884, the Japanese had begun to regain their confidence and look with skepticism on imports from the West. In the Rokumeikan, lofty officials and foreign dignitaries no longer waltzed in international accord. After the government had failed in 1887 to amend the treaties with the Western nations to the satisfaction of its people, the building had been assigned to other uses. Kanzô agreed with the spirit of selfsufficiency that this change in emphasis reflected. “Can we not govern ourselves by laws made by our own politicians, and convert ourselves with God’s help only? Christianity Japan must have and will have; but only that Christianity that has grown upon her own soil, [is] watered by her own streams, nurtured in her own bosoms, and garbed ... in her own oriental attire.”

From among the jobs that were offered to him, Kanzô chose the one that promised the greatest independence. A group of Christian and other leaders in Niigata on the Japan Sea coast had organized a “college” to which they called him in the fall of 1888 as “president.” They wanted an institution Christian in tone but free of what they considered the more objectionable features of the schools operated by missionaries. They believed that missionaries used their schools as tools for evangelization. The distinction between a school that existed primarily to evangelize and one that had a Christian tone but did not exist to make converts was difficult to define and maintain. The task became even more formidable when the backers agreed to accept gratis local missionaries as English teachers. The missionaries rejoiced at the opportunity to gain new contacts in Japanese society. They were either told they could evangelize in the school or took it for granted they could. Lack of a firm decision on this issue invited conflict from those who disagreed.

The two protagonists in the ensuing conflict were a Dr. H. Scudder (182295) and Kanzô. Scudder had served many years in India, where missionaries had led in the development of the churches more than they had in Japan. This experience had not equipped Scudder to deal with a Japanese “native convert” – as he would have phrased it – with Kanzô’s capability and conviction. Disagreement followed Kanzô’s decision to invite a follower of the Japanese Buddhist saint Nichiren to address the school. Uchimura wanted the students to study the best in their own heritage before they tackled Christianity. The founders of the school sided with the missionaries, and Kanzô returned to Tokyo. His first position after coming home had confirmed his suspicion that foreigners did not respect Japanese. It had also strengthened his resolve to dispense with foreign assistance if at all possible.

In Tokyo, Kanzô could find only part-time jobs. He taught in small private schools, worked on some problems in fisheries science, and delivered occasional lectures. He married a second time. His wife Kazuko shared neither the education nor the outside interests of Take, but she seems to have satisfied Kanzô.

Early in 1889, they observed the celebrations in Tokyo that attended the promulgation of the new Constitution. To the “new” men of Japan like Kanzô, this marked a great step forward, both for Japan and for its image abroad. It now boasted a government similar to those of the most advanced nations and could take its place among them. The Christians in particular celebrated, for the Constitution guaranteed them freedom of belief in words that at the time seemed to imply a stable place in society.

A tragedy lessened their sense of accomplishment. On the same day the new Constitution went into effect, assassins took the life of Mori Arinori, the Westernized and capable minister of education. The motivation for the assassination was not known immediately. Kanzô concluded from it that the Japanese were not yet prepared to take on the responsibilities of popular government that the opening of the new national assembly, due to convene the following year, would bring.

Mori’s assassination marked the beginning of irrational outbreaks against the “new” men such as Mori and Kanzô. Mori had been proficient in English. He had befriended Westerners and Christians even though he may not have himself become a Christian, and while serving his government in the United States he had actively sought advice from authorities such as the president of Amherst College about what Japan should use as a basis for ethical training. He had stood out as an advocate of rapid change. He had fallen before an assassin. Kanzô, who resembled Mori in so many ways, had reason to fear similar physical violence.

Late in 1889, a few months after Mori’s death and a year before the Rescript on Education that would cause Uchimura so much trouble was promulgated, Kanzô delivered a speech that demonstrated how in fact typical of his day were his attitudes toward the great symbols of his nation. What he said there is remembered now because it contrasts with the image of the traitor that resulted from his later refusal to bow. He spoke to the students of a girls’ school in Azabu. One member of the audience recalled that Uchimura chose as his topic evidences of God’s favour to Japan. First he referred to the chrysanthemums that adorned the lecture platform to illustrate the beautiful botanical specimens in Japan; then he pointed out the window to the cone of Mount Fuji, visible on the clear horizon of a November day. He climaxed his talk with reference to the Imperial family, “the one great pride of the Japanese people.” No statement or act before his refusal to bow would have led any Japanese to suspect his loyalty.

The following fall Kanzô obtained his position at the First Higher School, the most prestigious high school in Japan. Those students who graduated from it moved on to Tokyo Imperial University. No high school teacher could ask for a better position. As a special lecturer, his income amounted to more than twice what he had received in Sapporo. This enabled him to rent a small home for his wife and himself near the school and away from his mother. Kanzô rejoiced at the abilities and deportment of his students. He lectured four times a week and oversaw study halls five hours. He also seems to have acted as a counsellor. Students could come to his house at will. “I will venture to teach in General History there,” he had written to Struthers. “I shall have abundance of opportunities for communicating to them the Life and Spirit of Him who saved me, through the medium of the History of the Christian Europe.”

At about the time that he started his lectures in the higher school, Kanzô bought a history that gave him ample material for such instruction. It was Thomas Carlyle’s Oliver Cromwell’s Letters and Speeches: With Elucidations. Although he had read through only half of the five volumes before the ceremony on 9 January 1891, when his refusal to bow made history, he had caught the spirit of moral rectitude that Carlyle evoked. The night before the ceremony he informed Miyabe in a letter that he wished to resign from the Sapporo church, apparently because he feared some act of his might implicate others by association.

The Rescript on Education set forth traditional ethical principles, largely Confucian, that had been drafted by advisors to Emperor Meiji. Fearing that exposure to foreign ideas might warp youthful minds and turn them away from their basic loyalties to Japan, the advisors intended this statement to provide a basis for ethical instruction in the schools. Their document emphasized, as a result, the moral precepts that members of Japanese society took for granted. Children were instructed to follow the traditional virtues so that they might “maintain the prosperity of Our Imperial Throne coeval with heaven and earth.” Each individual’s loyal observance of traditional ethical norms would together make the nation strong.

The text of the rescript had been made public late in 1890. The students and faculty members were not called together early in January to publicize its contents.
